W1-1.note: Every 'help' (broken basin, rags in papa's drawer, dust under dresses, cutting the lace) is damage the narrator cannot see, so the irony is the point of the passage.

W1-2.note: Papa says she 'won't wait to grow up' and makes 'the very best use of my time now'; C is what mamma says.

W1-3.note: A 'big pile' that Maria left when she went to answer the door implies she had swept it together and was interrupted, though the narrator's framing of Maria as careless makes E defensible to a reader.

W1-4.note: She plans to cut the lace off mamma's best walking suit to sew it better, which the reader sees will ruin it.

W1-5.note: A 'waist' with sleeves is the bodice or blouse of a period suit, not the middle of the body.

W1-6.note: She says Bessie 'isn't so much use as I am' and 'only plays while there's work going on'.

W2-1.note: Most of the passage is the narrator's distress at Father's veto and Mother's explanation that necessity, not lack of sympathy, drives it.

W2-2.note: Eleven dollars and twenty-five cents among fifteen girls is seventy-five cents apiece.

W2-3.note: Prompted by Mother's account of Father's money worries, the narrator wonders whether her mother silently does without things herself.

W2-4.note: She is to make the presentation address and thinks over 'what I should say', i.e. a formal speech.

W2-5.note: She wishes he would 'soften it a little' because 'a blunt no is a great deal harder to bear'.

W2-6.note: The aside contrasts Florence never thinking twice about a dollar with 'some of us', setting up why the cost is a burden.

W3-1.note: The violet calms them by pointing out that the copies have no fragrance and cannot renew themselves, as living flowers do.

W3-2.note: 'Worked in colored worsted' means embroidered in yarn.

W3-3.note: 'Oh, don't joke on such a subject' and the disapproving 'No' show they thought the matter too serious for a pun.

W3-4.note: She wishes the bee had been fooled because it would have 'served him right—the thief!', i.e. he steals her honey.

W3-5.note: The hubbub is the fuss the violet later calls 'a foolish fuss ... with no real cause'.

W3-6.note: The violet asks whether, when they fade, hidden blossoms will take the places of the dead ones; copies cannot.

W4-1.note: The author argues that 'bookworms' are common pests 'playing other roles' and that over thirty species, none worm-like, share the name.

W4-2.note: He failed to recognize that his two 'species' were the larva and imago of one species.

W4-3.note: The insects are met daily in the house and 'arouse no unusual interest' while people wonder what a bookworm is, so people meet them without knowing what they do.

W4-4.note: A 'curious and interesting characterization' is an odd, peculiar one (insects crowing like a cock).

W4-5.note: The author jokes about Mentzel's ear drums and 'an altogether different cock' from the kind we know.

W4-6.note: The question indicates a 'reaction against these weird and fantastical accounts', i.e. doubt.

W5-1.note: The seeming asters, cacti and chrysanthemums turn out to be flesh-eating animals whose petals are mouths.

W5-2.note: She praises the light from above and how 'complete is the illusion' that the glass is water.

W5-3.note: The stage is 'all around and about', lit from above, like the tanks lining the dark alleys on both sides.

W5-4.note: Calyx is a flower term, and she uses it even after learning the creatures are animals, while admitting she cannot tell whether a body exists.

W5-5.note: The keeper feeding 'his strange charges' means the creatures in his care, i.e. wards.

W5-6.note: The meat, 'now but a tiny ball of dry pulp, slowly sank to the bottom of the tank'.

W6-1.note: The author's central finding is that every source on freeze-thaw hoodoo formation traces back to Lindquist's single unpublished dissertation.

W6-2.note: Sediments washed into the lake from mountain streams and built up in layers to form the Claron limestone; the lake was 200 miles long, not deep.

W6-3.note: The website cites three works, but each credits the freeze-thaw idea to Lindquist.

W6-4.note: 'The greatest concentration of hoodoos found anywhere' means the densest cluster.

W6-5.note: She calls warming 'a grave threat' and fears we cannot adapt without the missing science, but the damage is prospective ('could', 'may').

W6-6.note: She contrasts the figurative 'reshaping' of attitudes and politics with the park being 'literally' reshaped.
